title: Infra playbook: GPU fleet, cloud accounts & networking, IaC modules, CI/CD (consolidated 2026)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:
This consolidated playbook describes Redwood Inference's recommended operational patterns for managing the GPU fleet and capacity, cloud accounts and networking configuration, Terraform/IaC module standards, CI/CD and build pipelines, and the set of infra runbooks the team must maintain. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for capacity planning, deployment automation, and day-2 operations.

Goals and scope:
- Provide a single reference for commonly executed capacity and deployment tasks.
- Standardize Terraform modules and CI/CD patterns used across GPU clusters, control plane services, and customer-dedicated environments.
- Reduce incident toil by documenting runbooks and ownership for high-risk procedures.

Ownership and SLAs:
- GPU Fleet Owner: infra-gpu-team@redwood.com (primary), eng-sre (secondary)
- Cloud Accounts & Networking: cloud-accounts-team@redwood.com
- IaC and CI/CD: infra-ci-team@redwood.com
- Target SLOs:
  - GPU allocation latency: 95th percentile < 45s for pre-warmed pools
  - Eviction rate (spot interruptions) handled by autoscaler < 2% per day
  - Provisioning success rate (Terraform apply) >= 98% in CI environments

High-level architecture and service map:
- GPU Fleet: managed in AWS (primary), GCP (secondary), with a unified abstraction layer (fleet-service) that exposes capacity APIs for route selection and quota accounting.
- Control plane services: k8s clusters for orchestration (cluster-a: us-east-1, cluster-b: europe-west-1).
- Networking: VPC per environment (prod/stage/dev) with transit-gateway for cross-region control plane connectivity, dedicated VPCs for customer-private deployments.
- IaC: Terraform mono-repo (infra-terraform/) with a module registry (git tags) and a gating policy enforced in CI.

1) GPU fleet & capacity management
Overview:
- We operate two capacity tiers: Reserved (dedicated) and Shared (hosted/spot-backed). The autoscaler and routing layer maintain headrooms for both tiers and handle pre-warming for predictable low-latency workloads.

Capacity planning procedure (quarterly):
1. Pull usage reports: tokens/sec, model mix, avg seq length from observability (console -> per-model dashboard).
2. Forecast demand using 3-month rolling median + 20% buffer for growth or model rollouts.
3. Map capacity to instance types (A100-40GB for high-memory models, H200 for high-throughput variants) and validate GPU SKU availability with cloud accounts team.
4. Submit capacity requests (PR to infra-requests repo) and schedule procurement or cloud quota increases.

Pre-warm policy and thresholds:
- Pre-warm target: maintain 10% headroom of reserved capacity for each SLA tier during business hours (09:00-18:00 in region local time).
- Scale-up trigger: sustained CPU/GPU utilization > 70% for 5 minutes OR queue length > 50k tokens for 2 minutes.
- Scale-down cooldown: 10 minutes to avoid thrashing.

Metric table (for capacity runbook):
- Metric: allocation_latency_95p, Target: <45s
- Metric: gpu_utilization_95p, Target: <75%
- Metric: pod_restart_rate_1h, Target: <0.5%

2) Cloud accounts and networking patterns
Network layout checklist (for every environment):
- VPC per environment with clear naming: vpc-{env}-{region} (e.g., vpc-prod-use1).
- Subnets segmented: control-plane (private), workloads (private), egress-nat (private with NAT GW), public-bastion.
- Transit and peering: use transit-gateway for prod cross-region; avoid per-customer peering unless required by compliance.
- Security groups: deny-by-default with explicitly allowed ports (SSH only from bastion, service ports on internal CIDRs).

Cloud accounts governance:
- IAM roles standardized: infra-deployer, infra-auditor, infra-operator.
- Account bootstrap: use account-bootstrap Terraform module (see IaC section) to provision baseline resources and guardrails (CloudTrail, Config, centralized logging).
- Quotas: owners must confirm vCPU, GPU quota increases 2 weeks before planned capacity changes.

Networking runbook (incident checklist):
1. Validate route tables and NAT gateways in affected VPC.
2. Check transit-gateway attachments and propagated routes.
3. Verify security group changes in last 24 hours (audit trails).
4. If connectivity lost to GPU nodes, attempt controlled reboot and inspect kernel-level logs, escalate to cloud provider support if stuck.

3) Terraform / IaC module standards
Repository layout and versioning:
- Monorepo: infra-terraform/ with directories: modules/, envs/, examples/, ci/
- Module versioning: semantic tags (vX.Y.Z) and changelog entries required for any public module change.
- Module contract: every module must include README, inputs.tf, outputs.tf, examples, and a stability label (alpha|beta|stable).

Required modules (short list):
- module/gpu-instance-pool (autoscaler-friendly group abstraction)
- module/account-bootstrap (logging, monitoring, baseline IAM)
- module/vpc-networking (VPC, subnets, route tables, NGW)
- module/k8s-cluster (EKS/GKE bootstrap settings)

Terraform best practices and checks (CI gates):
- Enforced: terraform fmt, tflint, tfsec, terraform validate.
- Policy checks: OPA policy evaluating IAM, public S3 buckets, and encryption at rest.
- Plan approval: non-trivial changes (any create/destroy of compute resources) require two approvers and a runbook entry describing rollback strategy.

IaC example snippet (gpu pool module usage):
module "gpu_pool_prod" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-terraform.git//modules/gpu-instance-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "gpu-pool-prod-a"
  instance_type = "nvidia-a100-40gb"
  desired_count = 40
  spot_enabled  = true
}

4) CI/CD and build patterns for infra
Pipeline goals:
- Fast, deterministic Terraform plan/apply in CI with strong gating to avoid production blast radius.
- Immutable artifact builds for control-plane services (docker images with SHA tags).
- Canary & gradual rollout support for infra changes (e.g., node AMI updates).

Pipeline stages (recommended):
1. Lint & static checks: terraform fmt, tflint, go vet, unit tests.
2. Build artifacts: packer/ami build or docker image build, push to registry with immutability checks.
3. Plan: terraform plan in a transient workspace, upload plan for review.
4. Approvals: automated owner check + manual approver for changes touching prod.
5. Apply: run in a controlled agent with scoped credentials and limited concurrency.
6. Post-apply verification: smoke tests, health checks, and dashboard validation.

CI patterns for GPU images and drivers:
- Build GPU AMI images using Packer with two-layer testing: unit (packer validate) and integration (spin a small instance with tests that validate driver, CUDA, and runtime libraries).
- Image promotion: images must pass integration tests and be promoted with an immutable tag (release-YYYYMMDD-<sha>).

5) Runbooks and operational playbooks (day-2 scenarios)
Runbook: GPU node OOM / model crashes
1. Identify affected node(s) via monitoring (node-exporter, GPU exporter).
2. Drain node: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node>
3. Collect diagnostics: /var/log/messages, dmesg, nvidia-smi --query, container runtime logs.
4. If memory leak observed, roll back recent deployment for model-serving pods and force-recreate pods on other nodes.
5. Submit post-incident note and update the regression set in applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks.

Runbook: Terraform plan/apply fails in prod CI
1. Do not apply ad-hoc fixes. Recreate plan with debug logging: TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan.
2. Check state-lock (DynamoDB) status and resolve stale locks.
3. If plan indicates destructive changes, open an incident with infra owners and follow approval matrix.

6) CI/CD rollback and canary strategy for infra changes
- Canary window: apply to a single region and validate: health checks, allocation latency, and unit cost within 10% of baseline.
- Automated rollback conditions: values out of SLO for 2 consecutive 5-minute windows (e.g., allocation_latency_95p > 90s).

7) Documentation & team wiki hygiene
- Every module and runbook must include an owner, last-reviewed date, and a short test checklist. Use the template:
  - Owner: team-name
  - Last reviewed: YYYY-MM-DD
  - Smoke tests: list of commands/metrics to run after change

Template example (module README):
| Field | Value |
| Owner | infra-ci-team |
| Stability | stable |
| Last reviewed | 2026-11-01 |
| Smoke test | terraform plan -> assert no unintended destroy |

8) Incident escalation matrix and contacts
- Pager escalation: infra-gpu primary -> eng-sre secondary -> oncall-manager tertiary.
- Pager hours: primary oncall 24/7 for prod. Use #pager-duty Slack channel for incident comms.

Appendices
A. Quick commands
- Check GPU utilization: kubectl exec -it <pod> -- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu --format=csv
- Drain node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- Terraform plan in CI: TF_VAR_env=prod make ci-terraform-plan

B. Example Terraform module CI pipeline (short YAML excerpt):
jobs:
  terraform-plan:
    steps:
      - checkout
      - setup-terraform
      - run: terraform init
      - run: terraform fmt -check
      - run: tflint
      - run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
      - upload-artifact: plan.tfplan

C. Related pages and references
- infra-terraform module registry (internal git)
- gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026 (operational runbook)
- infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026 (detailed design)

Contact and feedback
- For addition or correction requests, open a PR against infra-terraform/docs or file a ticket in the infra-team backlog tagged "documentation".
